analysis.one_liner: Removes the legal shield that protects government officials from lawsuits for violating constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and died without a vote at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: When a police officer or other government official violates someone's constitutional rights, a judge-made doctrine called "qualified immunity" usually blocks the victim from winning money damages unless they can show the right was already "clearly established" in prior court cases. This bill would wipe out that defense for lawsuits brought under the 1871 civil rights statute, making officials personally answerable in court for rights violations no matter what they believed at the time. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2023 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by state and local officials — most often in police misconduct cases — who currently lose their lawsuits because they cannot point to a prior court case with identical facts. The bill would let juries decide damages based on the facts of the case itself.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the 1871 civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) so that a defendant cannot escape liability by claiming they acted in good faith, believed their conduct was lawful, or that the right violated was not "clearly established" [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings state that qualified immunity is a judicial invention not found in the 1871 statute itself, created by Supreme Court decisions in 1967 and 1982, and that it has "severely limited the ability of many plaintiffs to recover damages" [S3].
It applies to lawsuits pending on or filed after enactment, so people whose cases are already in court could benefit immediately [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Police officers and other government officials who violate constitutional rights would face personal money judgments, and the cities and counties that employ and indemnify them would pay most of those judgments and the added liability insurance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police, other officials, and local governments

drawbacks.text: Government employee groups argue that eliminating qualified immunity would subject officials to personal liability for split-second decisions, making it harder to recruit and retain police officers [widely reported; not in provided sources].

The bill's text notes that the immunity doctrine shields officials; removing it entirely means even officials who honestly but mistakenly believed their conduct was legal would be liable, with no good-faith safety valve [S3].
Municipalities, which typically indemnify their employees, would absorb most of the cost, which would fall back on local taxpayers through insurance premiums and settlements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill restores what its sponsors say was the original meaning of a statute Congress passed in 1871, giving victims of rights violations a realistic path to a courtroom instead of a doctrinal dead end. The main honest cost is increased liability for individual officials and the local governments that back them, and supporters of the current doctrine argue some protection is needed for officials making fast decisions under uncertainty. The bill offers no middle ground — it removes the defense entirely.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2023 and stayed there; the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on April 19, 2023, joined by Senators Sanders and Warren [S1] [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
The Senate action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government officials and the police departments and local governments that benefit from qualified immunity are better off because the bill never advanced; no court case or cost of liability changed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only three Senate supporters, all progressive Democrats or allied independents, and no Republican support is recorded; it never reached a vote where party positions would have been counted.

industries.note: Officers would lose the judicial shield that ends most civil rights lawsuits before a jury hears them, and departments would face more litigation and higher insurance costs. Their interest in keeping the defense runs against the interest of people seeking compensation for rights violations.
Cities and counties generally pay judgments against their employees, so ending qualified immunity would raise their settlement, verdict, and insurance costs.
More claims and higher exposure would mean more premiums written and a larger market for coverage of government entities.
